candidateRows: Libertarian freedom preserves the idea that agents genuinely affect the world, whereas compatibilism leaves events proceeding without choices making that deeper difference.
This supplies Hawkins's central positive motivation for libertarianism and identifies the specific feature he considers absent from the compatibilist account.
After outlining standard positions, Hawkins explains his own commitment by connecting agency with everyday intelligibility and with choices making a genuine difference.
Arguments against libertarian freedom depend on contestable physicalist assumptions, while agency is a pervasive datum that a satisfactory worldview must explain rather than dismiss.
The move establishes his methodological burden of proof against naturalism and argues that libertarianism need not conflict with contemporary physical science.
Hawkins rejects physics-first closure assumptions, treats experienced agency as explanatory data, and notes that physicalist libertarian accounts remain available.
Complete knowledge of every physical state and natural law would permit derivation of all subsequent events, apparently excluding genuine alternative possibilities.
This states the principal determinist pressure the pro case must answer: whether law-governed physical prediction rules out the ability to do otherwise.
Hawkins's claim that libertarian agency is coherent and not defeated by physicalism.
Following Hawkins's rejection of physicalist closure assumptions, Folley formulates a Laplace-style challenge based on exhaustive physical information and laws.
Causal determinism threatens not only moral responsibility but rational normativity, because every belief and inference would be merely caused rather than answerable to standards.
This is a direct rebuttal to determinist pressure and advances a self-undermining objection against treating all reasoning as causally compelled.
Folley's Laplace-style argument that laws and complete physical states determine every action.
Hawkins answers the determinist challenge by extending its consequences from responsibility to the standards distinguishing correct reasoning from merely actual thought.
Logical and mathematical standards must remain independent of how human beings are psychologically caused to think, or valid and invalid inference cannot be distinguished.
The move supplies the detailed normative premise needed for Hawkins's claim that causal determinism undermines warranted reasoning, including reasoning for determinism.
Folley's request to explain why determined reasoning would undermine reasons for believing determinism.
Using the distinction between psychology and logic, Hawkins argues that objective standards govern how people ought to infer despite how they actually think.
A causally determined argument would coincide with objective reasoning only accidentally, so avoiding self-defeat requires removing coercive causation from determinism.
This sharpens the earlier normativity objection and distinguishes noncausal determinacy from a picture in which thought is forced or inescapably produced.
Folley's formulation that normative reasons fail if a person could not have reasoned otherwise.
After Folley summarizes the normativity concern, Hawkins contends that compelled reasoning cannot itself justify causal determinism and isolates causation as the problem.
A world-encompassing predictor faces regress or contradiction if its own predictions are included among the states it must predict.
The predictor problem attacks a key premise of the Laplacean challenge by questioning whether complete prediction can coherently include the predicting process itself.
Folley's challenge that universal causation and law-based prediction may follow from inexpensive assumptions.
Hawkins revisits the imagined demon and argues that including its predictions within the predicted world generates loops that threaten the model's coherence.

Determinist arguments illicitly import temporal priority and constraint even though time-symmetric physical equations provide mathematical interconnection without showing that the past forces the future.
This directly separates physical determinacy from causal compulsion and challenges the naturalist inference from reversible laws to a future constrained by the past.
The Laplacean claim that past states and natural laws already determine and constrain every later action.
Hawkins contrasts open-future rhetoric with tenseless physics, observes that equations run in both temporal directions, and questions imported notions of forcing.
Abstract physical determinacy is noncausal and perspective-free, while experimental causation is intervention-relative and grounded in agents' deliberative ability to manipulate conditions.
The distinction underwrites Hawkins's reconciliation of explanatory determinism with agency by denying that mathematical relations entail past-directed causal constraint.
Folley's request to identify which concepts of causation support causal determinism and which fall short.
Hawkins separates atemporal mathematical relations from defeasible experimental interventions, arguing that causal selection reflects agents' interests and manipulable alternatives.
Even noncausal determinism appears to eliminate libertarian branching possibilities when fixed laws and past states uniquely determine both future and past states.
This preserves the central determinist objection after Hawkins rejects causal language, asking whether mathematical uniqueness alone defeats the ability to do otherwise.
Hawkins's distinction between acceptable explanatory determinism and constraining causal determinism.
Folley grants that physical equations may be temporally symmetric but argues that unique law-governed evolution still undermines a garden of branching alternatives.
Forking-path libertarianism requires indeterminism, but physicalist accounts can supply it through quantum effects and top-down causation.
The move directly answers whether branching alternatives survive determinist pressure and identifies a physicalist route to genuine alternatives.
Folley's challenge that non-causal determinism still eliminates branching alternatives and the ability to have done otherwise.

After Folley asks whether the branching-tracks picture can be salvaged, Hawkins distinguishes his preferred view from standard forking-path libertarianism while explaining how physicalists defend the latter.
Brain-level criteria can constrain quantum indeterminacy so that decisions remain reason-responsive without becoming either determined or random.
It addresses the randomness objection to libertarian choice by describing a mechanism combining alternative possibilities with rational constraint.
Folley's concern that indeterminism may not preserve the libertarian ability to choose among genuinely branching possibilities.
Hawkins uses radioactive decay as an analogy, then describes a neurophysiological theory in which prior decisions configure criteria that constrain but do not determine later choices.
Top-down causation rejects microreductionism because macro-level patterns help determine micro-events and informational patterns evade ordinary closure assumptions.
The move supplies the anti-reductionist causal architecture needed for the preceding physicalist defense of nonrandom libertarian agency.
Folley's characterization of the physicalist proposal as a rejection of exhaustive micro-level reductionism.

Following Folley's summary of the view, Hawkins explains reciprocal upward and downward causation and argues that pattern-level information is not governed by conservation principles in the same way as particles.
Indeterminism can reappear at the psychological level even when intermediate physical levels are deterministic, making decision-level freedom conceptually coherent.
It independently supports the coherence of decision-level indeterminism and weakens the inference from lower-level determination to determined agency.
Folley's observation that the cited neurophysical account differs from Hawkins's own non-branching libertarian position.
Hawkins invokes multi-level modeling to argue that determinism and indeterminism can alternate across descriptive scales, with psychologically described decisions remaining indeterminate.
Libertarian freedom needs sourcehood and alternative possibilities, but alternative possibilities do not require an objectively branching future.
This states Hawkins's central libertarian alternative to both causal determinism and the standard forking-path model challenged by Folley.
Folley's request to distinguish Hawkins's own view from a branching-tracks form of physicalist libertarianism.
Hawkins separates sourcehood from the ability to do otherwise, appeals to scientific modal reasoning, and permits a different past in the possible world where a different choice occurs.
Hawkins's modal claim may not conflict with the consequence argument because changing the decision by changing the past concedes that a fixed past fixes the decision.
It challenges whether Hawkins has answered determinist pressure or merely changed the modal scope by allowing the antecedent past to vary.
Hawkins's claim that one could have chosen otherwise in a possible world whose past and initial conditions were also different.
Folley reconstructs the consequence argument using fixed past facts and natural laws, then asks where any real disagreement remains if Hawkins varies those fixed conditions.
The consequence argument wrongly transfers logical dependence from past to present into dependence of agency, control, and sourcehood.
This is the principal idealist-libertarian response to the consequence argument, separating atemporal possibility from causally interpreted control.
Folley's objection that Van Inwagen can accept different choices under different pasts while still denying alternatives when the actual past is fixed.

Hawkins argues that alternative possibility is atemporal, whereas manipulability and sourcehood arise within agential causal reasoning; logical implication therefore cannot by itself transmit lack of control.
Hawkins and Van Inwagen use 'could have done otherwise' at different modal scopes, and both usages can coexist without contradiction.
The move argues that Hawkins has not refuted the determinist formulation because his broader possible-world quantification answers a different question.
Hawkins's charge that the consequence argument illegitimately combines logical implication with the agential concepts of control and sourcehood.
Folley grants counterfactual variation across worlds but maintains that Van Inwagen restricts attention to worlds sharing the actual past and laws, making the two claims compatible.
Causal determinism trivially excludes branching futures, but libertarian freedom can persist under non-causal determinism by combining modal alternatives with agential sourcehood.
The move clarifies the precise incompatibility claim and presents the dual-perspective framework Hawkins regards as sufficient for libertarian free will.
Folley's contention that fixed-past branching and broader possible-world alternatives are compatible but distinct uses of modal language.

Hawkins says branching libertarians simply reject causal determinism, then argues that idealism can retain both timeless logical possibility and situated pragmatic agency without fully reducing either perspective to the other.
Causation is fundamentally an agency-based concept of influence and reasons, so importing mechanistic necessity into it creates a false threat to free will.
This supplies the idealist foundation for preferring non-causal determination: rational structure explains events without turning agents into externally forced puppets.
Folley's request for clarification about whether Hawkins's definition of libertarian free will is broader than Van Inwagen's branching conception.

Hawkins distinguishes causal from non-causal determinism, treats deliberators as sources within pragmatic reasoning, and traces causation from agential influence through theological and mechanistic reinterpretations to formal causation.
Non-causal determinism does not establish the consequence argument's conclusion because logical dependence cannot determine causal control or agential sourcehood.
This directly defends libertarian agency against a determinist argument by separating logical entailment from the causal and practical concepts of control and sourcehood.
Folley's proposal to recast the consequence argument using non-causal determinism.

Folley asks whether a non-causal version of the consequence argument could coexist with libertarian freedom; Hawkins accepts the picture but rejects its inference from fixed propositions to absent control.
Non-causal determinism offers a stronger and more attractive basis for compatibilism because predictability need not imply causal puppeteering.
The move supplies the con side's core metaphysical alternative, retaining determinism while removing the causal-compulsion picture that motivates incompatibilist concern.

After agreeing that logical dependence differs from control, Folley presents non-causal determinism as the foundation of his compatibilism and locates determinism's unsettling force in complete external predictability.
Free will should be understood functionally through the distinctions needed to allocate incentives, prediction, praise, and blame even in a deterministic society.
This is the central compatibilist-pragmatist case: meaningful freedom survives metaphysical determinism because social and deliberative practices require graded distinctions among kinds of action.

Folley argues that free will has multiple practical meanings, using punishment, reflexes, premeditated murder, brain tumors, and coercion to show why agents must distinguish behavior by responsiveness and utility.
Agency remains indispensable in practice, and even complete foreknowledge can be passive while actions are still causally attributable to choosing agents.
The response absorbs the pragmatic need for responsibility into the pro case while arguing that prediction or foreknowledge does not displace the agent as the source of action.
Folley's functional account of freedom as allocating incentives, praise, blame, and useful behavioral distinctions.

Hawkins agrees that society cannot live without agency distinctions, then compares physical prediction with passive divine foreknowledge and argues that deliberation does not treat decisions as predetermined causal links.
Bradleyan idealism accepts scientific truths while rejecting the unsupported naturalist claim that scientific truths exhaust reality.
This establishes the idealist half of the pro position by challenging reductive naturalism and requiring metaphysics to integrate scientific, moral, aesthetic, religious, and agential experience.
Folley's request for Bradley's beliefs and for an explanation of how his idealism differs from other idealist traditions.

Hawkins places British idealism amid nineteenth-century scientific upheaval, accepts scientific discovery, rejects the added exclusivity premise, and presents Bradley's systematic metaphysics of the whole of experience.
Bradley improves on Hegel by treating reality as richer than rational thought, with feeling and volition preceding intellectual systematization.
The move identifies the distinctive Bradleyan basis for accommodating agency, value, and aesthetics and explains why intellectual science cannot constitute a complete account of reality.

Hawkins argues that direct felt engagement precedes rational modeling, uses infant experience as support, and contends that science and philosophy deliberately omit agential, ethical, and aesthetic dimensions.
A naturalistically acceptable idealism can treat experience as the subject matter and physical stuff as a model constructed from experience.
This offers the con side a naturalist-friendly appropriation of idealism, narrowing the dispute by denying that an experience-first ontology requires mysterious mental substances or anti-naturalism.
Hawkins's presentation of Bradleyan idealism as a broader alternative to reductive and thought-centered accounts.

After Hawkins affirms Folley's phenomenological reconstruction, Folley distinguishes mental-substance claims from an experience-centered methodology and characterizes physical objects as useful models of experience.
Idealism is philosophically pervasive because inquiry cannot bypass experience and judgment, but Bradley further requires inquiry to move beyond thought and language.

The move directly contrasts Bradleyan idealism with naturalistic phenomenalism and argues that consciousness, reference, agency, morality, and aesthetics expose the limits of exclusively intellectual explanation.
Folley's proposal that experience-first phenomenalism is already a fully naturalistic and metaphysically modest form of idealism.

Hawkins argues that the historical anomaly is the attempted leap beyond experience, cites pressures in mind and language, and explains Bradley's interwoven intellectual, moral, aesthetic, and felt modes of engagement.
Idealism need not imply conscious control over reality, but Bradley's appeal to an unstructured felt real risks conflicting with the unavoidable categorization built into perception.
The move distinguishes perspective-dependence from voluntary mental control while pressing whether Bradley's account can accommodate cognitively structured perception.
The preceding idealist account that truth remains wholly within experience and that feeling encounters reality directly.
After Hawkins argues that thought and feeling never escape experience, Folley grants ordinary mind-framing but questions whether any accessible experience is genuinely prior to categorization.
Bradleyan truth resembles operational coherence plus further constraints from felt reality and intellectual satisfaction, so idealism does not make truth whatever one chooses to think.
This response supplies a constraint on idealist truth that answers the charge of arbitrary coherence and connects thought to action, feeling, and practical failure.
Folley's concern that mind-framed truth may look mentally controllable or reducible to an arbitrarily coherent system.
Hawkins invokes operational coherence to explain why a merely consistent imagined world is not actual: attempts to act on false claims encounter failure and force revision.
Reflective agents cannot consciously recover wholly unstructured experience, yet precognitive feeling remains the foundation of thought and is ultimately integrated with structure in the absolute.
The move answers the perceptual-categorization objection while explaining how Bradley avoids identifying ultimate reality with either raw feeling alone or discursive structure alone.
Folley's objection that perception appears categorically structured from the outset and offers no accessible stage of unchopped experience.

Hawkins concedes that metacognitive reflection always structures experience, treats raw feeling as an inaccessible foundation, and locates completed truth in a union of feeling, thought, and volition.
Bradley's absolute requires clarification because it may be either a Peircean regulative ideal for inquiry or an independently real endpoint whose existence Bradley confidently affirms.
The question isolates whether the absolute performs only a methodological role or adds a substantive metaphysical commitment beyond pragmatic inquiry.
Hawkins's claim that complete truth culminates in the absolute where thought, feeling, goodness, and beauty finally unite.
Folley compares Bradley's endpoint with Peirce's indefinitely approached perfect theory and asks whether the absolute must actually exist rather than merely guide inquiry.
Bradley is not agnostic about the absolute: complete truth must exceed thought, and the normative drive toward truth already recognizes the greater reality of its fulfillment.
The response defends the substantive reality of the idealist endpoint by grounding it in the normativity and intelligibility of inquiry rather than treating it as a convenient fiction.
Folley's comparison of the absolute with Peirce's possibly unreal regulative ideal and his question about Bradley's certainty.
Hawkins argues that a settled theory cannot itself be complete reality, but inquiry's orientation toward fulfillment treats that completion as more real than present partial understanding.
The absolute may be understood more modestly as the amplified practical presupposition that intellectual, moral, and aesthetic progress are possible.
The move proposes a pragmatist reconstruction of the absolute that preserves its action-guiding role while testing whether stronger metaphysical claims are necessary.
Hawkins's argument that normative striving recognizes the absolute as a genuinely real completion rather than a mere fiction.
Folley compares faith in the absolute with researchers' disposition to assume that a solution is possible, extending the analogy across intellectual, aesthetic, and moral progress.
Inquiry presupposes an intelligible attainable end, and idealism makes this intelligibility less accidental by joining knower and known rather than positing an inaccessible independent reality.
The move argues that idealism explains the possibility and direction of inquiry better than a naturalistic picture containing realities that may be wholly disconnected from experience.
Folley's proposal that the absolute is simply the practical faith presupposed whenever people pursue intellectual, moral, or aesthetic progress.
Hawkins accepts the presuppositional analogy but argues that Bradley treats the goal as real because it directs inquiry and because reality cannot be separated from experiential relations.
Philosophical theories are shaped by the questions and aims they serve, so reductive claims that one theory exhausts reality illegitimately exclude aspects they cannot explain.
The argument directly resists naturalist reduction by tying theoretical adequacy to inquiry's purposes while preserving rigorous investigation of realities beyond any single framework.
Hawkins describes an insight about question-relative theorizing that led him away from desert-landscape reductionism toward rigorous but open-ended attempts to account for experience as a whole.
Anti-reductionism still requires defensible admission standards, because inquiry must avoid both scientistic exclusion and an unrestricted free-for-all.
The move states the compatibilist-pragmatist pressure on expansive idealism: openness to phenomena must be paired with standards that constrain what inquiry accepts.
Hawkins's rejection of reductive theories and his call to pursue comprehensive philosophy without dismissing what a theory cannot explain.
Folley agrees that scientism can be too restrictive but retains its demand for standards, presenting the selection of non-reductive yet non-permissive criteria as the central difficulty.
Bradley and William James share substantial pragmatist ground, but Bradley treats experienced urges toward truth and morality as evidence of an ultimate reality that genuinely draws inquiry onward.
The distinction locates the remaining divide between pragmatism and Bradleyan idealism in whether normative striving is merely an urge or discloses a real metaphysical source.
Folley's proposal that pragmatic standards offer a middle course between scientistic reduction and unrestricted philosophical permissiveness.
Hawkins notes Bradley's acknowledged similarity to James, then explains that Bradley moves beyond the mere existence of truth-seeking urges to posit something real that urges agents.
